system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2127-03-13 01:12:00 to 2127-03-14 19:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes and chronic gastroparesis was admitted for worsening abdominal pain and nausea, consistent with a gastroparesis flare triggered by back pain and anxiety. She presented with severe pain and dehydration, requiring IV fluids and pain control. Her symptoms improved with treatment, and she was able to tolerate a full diet by discharge. Labs showed elevated creatinine at 2.0, which decreased to 1.8 but remained concerning for possible progression of diabetic nephropathy. Lisinopril was discontinued due to kidney concerns, and amlodipine was started for blood pressure management. Sinus tachycardia, likely due to pain and anxiety, improved with symptom control. She was discharged home with plans for nephrology follow-up and continuation of her diabetes and psychiatric medications.

diagnoses.long_title: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Diabetes with ophthalmic manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, benign, with chronic kidney disease stage I through stage IV, or unspecified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the hospital because you were having severe nausea and vomiting. Do you remember coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I felt so sick. I couldn’t stay awake. I’ve had this before with my stomach—gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Given your history of type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis, this looks like a flare-up. You were very drowsy when you arrived, so we couldn’t talk much then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry. I just couldn’t keep my eyes open. Was my blood sugar high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 289 when you arrived. We started you on IV fluids and adjusted your insulin because you weren’t able to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh good. I was worried I might’ve done something wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. These flares can happen even with good care. We’ve been monitoring your labs. Your kidney function is a concern—we saw your creatinine was 1.7, which is elevated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? That’s from my diabetes, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s part of diabetic kidney disease. But it’s stable for now. We’re keeping an eye on it. Your blood pressure was high too—161 over 114.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I missed a few doses of my blood pressure meds. I’ve been so nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain it. We restarted your lisinopril and amlodipine. Your pressure is coming down now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll try not to miss them again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I’m not vomiting anymore. Still a little nauseous, but it’s much improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re going to try giving you small sips of water. If you keep that down, we’ll advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope I can eat soon. I hate being on IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get there. Your lipase was normal, so it’s not pancreatitis. And your liver tests are okay. This is likely a gastroparesis flare, possibly triggered by stress or a mild virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sister had a stomach bug recently, but she had diarrhea. I didn’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right, so it might not be the same thing. But stress and anxiety can also worsen gastroparesis. How have you been feeling mentally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Anxious, honestly. I get panic attacks, and being sick makes it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve continued your lorazepam, mirtazapine, and risperidone. Social work also checked in with you yesterday—they said you have good support at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my sister helps me a lot. I see my therapist weekly too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve kept down clear liquids and we’ve moved you to soft foods. Your blood sugar is 178 now—much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Should I be worried about my eyes or kidneys again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your retinopathy and kidney issues are chronic, but we’re managing them. The anemia we saw—your hemoglobin is 10.2—is something to watch, likely related to kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get tired easily. Is that from the anemia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll follow up with your PCP to check iron levels and consider treatment if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a full meal and kept it down. That’s a big step. The endocrinology team reviewed your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 28 units of 70/30 in the morning before. Is that changing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Temporarily, yes. While you weren’t eating, we used Lantus. Now that you’re back on meals, we’re switching you to 20 units with breakfast and 15 with dinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll need to adjust my sliding scale too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue checking your sugars four times a day and use your sliding scale as directed. Call your doctor if they’re consistently high or low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Your blood pressure is 138 over 99, and you’re alert and eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I feel so much better. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue lisinopril 20 mg and amlodipine 10 mg daily for blood pressure. Keep taking your psychiatric meds as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—20 units of 70/30 at breakfast, 15 at dinner. Make sure you eat when you take it to avoid low sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Do I need to see my specialists?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Follow up with your gastroenterologist and nephrologist. We’re also arranging an urgent endocrine appointment for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I’ll make sure to keep all my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and call if anything worsens—especially nausea, high sugars, or dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I worry about my back pain? It’s been acting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be contributing to your stress and nausea. Keep managing it with your usual plan, and mention it at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I will. And my vision—I’ve been seeing floaters lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your diabetic retinopathy, you should see your eye doctor soon. Report any sudden vision changes immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call them this week. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Stay hydrated, eat regularly, and keep your sugars in check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. It’s hard sometimes, but I’m trying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re here to support you. Let’s get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Dr. Lee. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon, hopefully not in the hospital!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fingers crossed. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on my way.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes and a history of gastroparesis, diabetic retinopathy, chronic kidney disease, and depression was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and altered mental status due to a gastroparesis flare. She presented with hyperglycemia, hypertension, and lethargy but improved with IV fluids, insulin adjustment, and symptom management. Her mental status normalized, she tolerated a full diet, and her vitals stabilized.
